# xcp: An extended cp

`xcp` is a (partial) clone of the Unix `cp` command. It is not intended as a
full replacement, but as a companion utility with some more user-friendly
feedback and some optimisations that make sense under certain tasks (see
below).

[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/xcp.svg?colorA=777777)](https://crates.io/crates/xcp) 
![Github Actions](https://github.com/tarka/xcp/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)
[![Packaging status](https://repology.org/badge/tiny-repos/xcp.svg)](https://repology.org/project/xcp/versions)

*Warning*: `xcp` is currently beta-level software and almost certainly contains
bugs and unexpected or inconsistent behaviour. It probably shouldn't be used for
anything critical yet.

Please note that there are some known issues with copying files from virtual
filesystems (e.g. `/proc`, `/sys`). See [this LWN
article](https://lwn.net/Articles/846403/) for an overview of some of the
complexities of dealing with kernel-generated files.  This is a common problem
with file utilities which rely on random access; for example `rsync` has the
same issue.

## Installation

### Cargo

`xcp` can be installed directly from `crates.io` with:
```
cargo install xcp
```

### Arch Linux

[`xcp`](https://aur.archlinux.org/packages/xcp/) is available on the Arch Linux User Repository. If you use an AUR helper, you can execute a command such as this:
```
yay -S xcp
```

### NetBSD
[`xcp`](https://pkgsrc.se/sysutils/xcp) is available on NetBSD from the official repositories. To install it, simply run:
```
pkgin install xcp
```

## Features and Anti-Features

### Features

* Displays a progress-bar, both for directory and single file copies. This can
  be disabled with `--no-progress`.
* On Linux it uses `copy_file_range` call to copy files. This is the most
  efficient method of file-copying under Linux; in particular it is
  filesystem-aware, and can massively speed-up copies on network mounts by
  performing the copy operations server-side. However, unlike `copy_file_range`
  sparse files are detected and handled appropriately.
* Support for modern filesystem features such as [reflinks](https://btrfs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Reflink.html).
* Optimised for 'modern' systems (i.e. multiple cores, copious RAM, and
  solid-state disks, especially ones connected into the main system bus,
  e.g. NVMe).
* Optional aggressive parallelism for systems with parallel IO. Quick
  experiments on a modern laptop suggest there may be benefits to parallel
  copies on NVMe disks. This is obviously highly system-dependent.
* Switchable 'drivers' to facilitate experimenting with alternative strategies
  for copy optimisation. Currently 2 drivers are available:
  * 'parfile': the previous hard-coded xcp copy method, which parallelises
    tree-walking and per-file copying. This is the default.
  * 'parblock': An experimental driver that parallelises copying at the block
    level. This has the potential for performance improvements in some
    architectures, but increases complexity. Testing is welcome.
* Non-Linux Unix-like OSs (OS X, *BSD) are supported via fall-back operation
  (although sparse-files are not yet supported in this case).
* Optionally understands `.gitignore` files to limit the copied directories.
* Optional native file-globbing.

### (Possible) future features

* Conversion of files to sparse where appropriate, as with `cp`'s
  `--sparse=always` flag.
* Aggressive sparseness detection with `lseek`.
* On non-Linux OSs sparse-files are not currenty supported but could be added if
  supported by the OS.

### Differences with `cp`

* Permissions, xattrs and ACLs are copied by default; this can be disabled with
  `--no-perms`.
* Virtual file copies are not supported; for example `/proc` and `/sys` files.
* Character files such as [sockets](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/unix.7.html) and
  [pipes](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/mkfifo.3.html) are copied as
  devices (i.e. via [mknod](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mknod.2.html))
  rather than copying their contents as a stream.
* The `--reflink=never` option may silently perform a reflink operation
  regardless. This is due to the use of
  [copy_file_range](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/copy_file_range.2.html)
  which has no such override and may perform its own optimisations.
* `cp` 'simple' backups are not supported, only numbered.
* Some `cp` options are not available but may be added in the future.

## Performance

Benchmarks are mostly meaningless, but the following are results from a laptop
with an NVMe disk and in single-user mode. The target copy directory is a git
checkout of the Firefox codebase, having been recently gc'd (i.e. a single 4.1GB
pack file). `fstrim -va` and `echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches` are
run before each test run to minimise SSD allocation performance interference.

Note: `xcp` is optimised for 'modern' systems with lots of RAM and solid-state
disks. In particular it is likely to perform worse on spinning disks unless they
are in highly parallel arrays.

### Local copy

* Single 4.1GB file copy, with the kernel cache dropped each run:
    * `cp`: ~6.2s
    * `xcp`: ~4.2s
* Single 4.1GB file copy, warmed cache (3 runs each):
    * `cp`: ~1.85s
    * `xcp`: ~1.7s
* Directory copy, kernel cache dropped each run:
    * `cp`: ~48s
    * `xcp`: ~56s
* Directory copy, warmed cache (3 runs each):
    * `cp`: ~6.9s
    * `xcp`: ~7.4s

### NFS copy

`xcp` uses `copy_file_range`, which is filesystem aware. On NFSv4 this will result
in the copy occurring server-side rather than transferring across the network. For
large files this can be a significant win:

* Single 4.1GB file on NFSv4 mount
    * `cp`: 6m18s
    * `xcp`: 0m37s

### AI Contribution Policy

This project will not accept runtime code generated by AI. Generation of _draft_
documentation and test code is acceptable, but should be reviewed by the
submitter before raising a PR.

    st=l[1].decode()
    rate=st[34:49]
    seen.setdefault(len(rate),set()).add(rate)
for k,v in sorted(seen.items()):
    print(k, len(v))
    for x in sorted(v)[:8]: print('  ',repr(x))

Very interesting! So there IS a draw per progress message. The burst frames show the bar filling up 1-2 chars at a time. That means the progress updates come at a rate of ~10MB per ms... hmm, with 200 blocks over 19ms, each block is 1MB. Each block → one frame? 200 blocks / 19ms → we see 21 frames in 19ms. Hmm, that's not 200.

Unless copy_file_range copies MORE than the requested block size in one call... no, 1MB per call.

Hmm, wait: 200 blocks over 19ms = 10.5 GB/s. Plausible for a fast SSD/tmpfs? Actually copy_file_range on overlayfs... The earlier test showed 200MB copied in ~0.15s with block-size 1?? no.

Hmm, let me reconsider: the frames show the bar filling by 1 char each ~1ms. The bar is 98 chars, and 200MB... 21 frames → the bar went from 0 to ~8 chars in 21 frames. 8/98 = 8% of 200MB = 16MB. Hmm.

So the messages come at ~1MB per message (each message = 1MB = one block)? Then 21 messages = 21MB in 19ms. Hmm, 200MB total would be 200 messages. But the run ended at 0.163s with 25 frames. So the copy completed in 0.163s and only 25 frames were drawn. So the copy loop sent 25 messages... but 200MB/1MB = 200 blocks.

Unless the copy loop sends a progress message per block but the driver coalesces? Hmm. OR: copy_file_range is called ONCE for the whole file (200MB) and the progress message is sent once! Then the "bar filling" would be a single jump.

Hmm, but we see gradual filling. So multiple messages.

Let me reconsider: maybe the copy loop uses a fixed internal buffer size (not the block size) for the read/write, and copy_file_range is called with the block size. Hmm.

Let me test with block-size 1 and a 4MB file: we saw 261 frames (from the earlier ptycap with wait=5). 4MB/1 = 4M blocks. 261 frames ≠ 4M. So NOT per block.

Hmm! So how many messages? Let me compute: in the ptytime run with block-size 1 and 13s: 226 chunks. The copy took ~11.4s. So ~226 messages in 11.4s. Hmm, so the message rate is ~20/s regardless of block size. That suggests the messages are NOT per block but throttled somehow, OR the drawing is throttled.

Hmm, but then what explains the burst of 21 frames in 19ms at the start? 

OH! Maybe the progress bar thread draws when the terminal is... Hmm.

Let me think about it differently: maybe the copy loop sends a progress message per block, and the drawing thread uses a *bounded* channel; when the channel is full, the sender blocks or drops. If the channel capacity is small (e.g., 1 or 2), and the drawing thread is slower... hmm.

Actually — here's a cleaner hypothesis: the progress thread is:

```rust
loop {
    let ev = rx.recv_timeout(REFRESH_INTERVAL)?;
    // drain?
    self.apply(ev);
    self.draw();
}
```
With `recv_timeout(50ms)`: if a message is available, apply and draw immediately. Since messages arrive fast (per block), each message → a draw → the rate would be limited by the message rate, not 50ms.

For block-size 1 (4M messages), we'd get millions of draws. We observed ~226 chunks in 13s. So no.

Hmm, so the messages must be throttled. How? Maybe the copy loop sends a progress message only every N bytes or every K blocks?

Alternatively — maybe the progress counter is an atomic shared value and the messages are only: "file started with total size", "file finished". Then how does the bar fill gradually? The draw thread polls the atomic every 50ms → 20/s ✓. And the burst?

Hmm, but the burst: at 0.002-0.019 there were 21 frames with the bar filling gradually. If the draw thread polls every 50ms, we'd see one frame at 0.002 (initial), then the next at 0.052.

Unless... the burst frames are drawn because the messages are: "total changed" (once), "progress" (each block)... 

Hmm, let me look at the 21 burst frames: the bar grew from 0 to 8 chars = 8% of 200MB = 16MB in 19ms. If the copy loop sends a message per 1MB block, 16 messages in 19ms ≈ 1MB/ms = 1GB/s. Plausible! Then the remaining 184 messages would also arrive fast... but only 3 more frames (at 50ms intervals) appear.

Hmm, so the drawing rate is ~1ms/frame for the first 21 frames then 50ms/frame. That's bizarre.

WAIT. Maybe it's the *rate calculation*! Maybe the progress message rate is throttled by the sender: the copy loop only sends a progress message if at least X ms have elapsed since the last send. Then:
- The first message: send immediately.
- Then the next message is sent when the elapsed time since the last *draw* exceeds something...

Hmm.

Alternatively, maybe the copy loop sends a message per block and the draw thread drains ALL pending messages but draws only once... no, we see 21 draws.

Hmm, let me reconsider. What if the copy loop's progress messages are sent per block, and the draw thread is:

```
loop {
   let ev = rx.recv()?;    // block until a message
   draw();
}
```
Then draws = messages. For block-size 1: 4M messages → 4M draws → we'd see a huge output. We saw 226 chunks. So no.

Unless the channel receiver coalesces: e.g., the sender uses `try_send` (dropping if full). Then the number of *received* messages = the number the receiver can process. With a bounded channel of capacity C, the sender blocks when full; the receiver drains and draws per message. The rate would be limited by the draw cost. Hmm, but we saw 50ms gaps, which is way slower than a draw.

OK, radical idea: maybe the progress messages are sent per *file*, and the "burst" is something else entirely. Let me test with multiple files of different sizes to see the pattern.

Actually — let me reconsider the burst: 21 frames in 19ms, the bar filling gradually by 1-2 chars. Then a 50ms gap, then a frame with the bar at 28 chars, then 37 chars...

Hmm! Look at the pattern: frames at 0.052 → 28 chars, 0.102 → 37, 0.152 → 37, 0.163 → 37 (the final). Hmm, 37/98 = 37.7% of 200MB = 75MB. And the copy completed at 0.163s.

So the last frame is at 100%? No, the bar shows 37 chars with the last at 0.163. Hmm, the final frame should be 100% (98 chars). Let me look at the actual stats lines of the last frames. Maybe the bar only shows the "current file" progress? No — for a single file the total is the file size.

Hmm, hold on: maybe the bar fill is based on the *rate* rather than the fraction? No.

Let me print the stats lines for all frames in this run to see.

Actually, I wonder: maybe the display shows the progress of the *current block*... no.

Let me just print all the frames' stats lines.

actions.command:
cd /tmp/t4 && cat > /tmp/pt5.py <<'EOF'
import os, pty, sys, select, time, subprocess, termios, struct, fcntl, re
m,s=pty.openpty()
fcntl.ioctl(s, termios.TIOCSWINSZ, struct.pack('HHHH', 24, 100, 0,0))
os.set_blocking(m, False)
p=subprocess.Popen(sys.argv[1:], stdin=s, stdout=s, stderr=s, close_fds=True)
t0=time.time(); buf=bytearray(); marks=[]
while time.time()-t0 < 25 and p.poll() is None:
    r,_,_=select.select([m],[],[],0.02)
    if r:
        try: d=os.read(m,65536)
        except OSError: break
        if d: marks.append((time.time()-t0, bytes(d))); buf+=d
p.kill()
data=bytes(buf)
seps=[(m.start(), m.end()) for m in re.finditer(rb'\x1b\[1A\r\x1b[2K\x1b[1B\r\x1b[2K\x1b[1A', data)]
frames=[]; prev=0
for st,en in seps:
    frames.append((prev, st)); prev=en
frames.append((prev, len(data)))
cum=0; si=0
# assign each frame a time = time when its last byte was written
acc=0
ti=0
times=[]
for (a,b) in frames:
    length=b-a
    while ti<len(marks)-1 and acc+marks[ti][1] <= a+b: acc+=marks[ti][1]; ti+=1
    times.append(marks[ti][0])
for (a,b),t in zip(frames,times):
    seg=data[a:b]
    parts=seg.split(b'\r\n')
    st=parts[-1] if len(parts)>1 else b''
    print('%.3f'%t, len(seg), repr(st.decode()[:60]))
EOF
rm -f o14 && timeout 60 python3 /tmp/pt5.py /workspace/executable --reflink never --block-size 1000000 -w 1 big o14 2>&1 | head -30

import re, collections
seen=collections.Counter()
for f in ['/tmp/pty.raw','/tmp/pty2.raw','/tmp/dp60c.raw']:
    try: data=open(f,'rb').read()
    except: continue
    for sep in [b'\x1b[1A\r\x1b[2K\x1b[1B\r\x1b[2K\x1b[1A', b'\x1b[2A\r\x1b[2K\x1b[1B\r\x1b[2K\x1b[1B\r\x1b[2K\x1b[2A']:
        pass
    frames=data.split(b'\x1b[1A\r\x1b[2K\x1b[1B\r\x1b[2K\x1b[1A')
    for fr in frames:
        parts=fr.split(b'\r\n')
        if len(parts)<2: continue
        st=parts[1].decode('utf8','replace')
        pi=[i for i,c in enumerate(st) if c=='|']
        if len(pi)<3: continue
        rate=st[pi[1]+1:pi[2]]
        seen[rate]+=1
# print a selection sorted by the numeric value
def val(s):
    m=re.match(r'\s*([\d.]+) (\w+)/s', s)
    if not m: return 0
    u=m.group(2)
    mult={'B':1,'KiB':1024,'MiB':1024**2,'GiB':1024**3,'TiB':1024**4}.get(u,1)
    return float(m.group(1))*mult
items=sorted(seen, key=val)
print(len(items))
for r in items[:3]+items[10:16]+items[-6:]:
    m=re.match(r'^(\s*)(.*?)(\s*)$', r, re.S)
    print(repr(r), 'L',len(m.group(1)), 'T',len(m.group(3)), 'mid',repr(m.group(2)))
PY"}

        set_xattr(to, &name, &value)?;
    }
    Ok(())

//! Command line handling.
//!
//! The command is built with the `clap` builder interface (rather than the
//! derive macro) which keeps the dependency graph small and matches the way
//! the original tool is written.

use std::path::PathBuf;

use crate::errors::*;
use crate::parse::{parse_block_size, BackupMode, Driver, ReflinkMode};

/// Version of the tool.
pub const VERSION: &str = "0.24.3";

/// Parsed command line arguments.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct Args {
    /// Positional path arguments.
    pub paths: Vec<PathBuf>,
    /// Number of `-v` flags seen.
    pub verbose: u8,
    /// Copy directories recursively.
    pub recursive: bool,
    /// Dereference symlinks in the source.
    pub dereference: bool,
    /// Number of parallel workers.
    pub workers: usize,
    /// Block size.
    pub block_size: u64,
    /// Do not overwrite an existing file.
    pub no_clobber: bool,
    /// Force (compatibility only).
    pub force: bool,
    /// Honour .gitignore files.
    pub gitignore: bool,
    /// Expand filename patterns.
    pub glob: bool,
    /// Disable the progress bar.
    pub no_progress: bool,
    /// Do not copy permissions.
    pub no_perms: bool,
    /// Do not copy timestamps.
    pub no_timestamps: bool,
    /// Copy ownership.
    pub ownership: bool,
    /// Selected driver.
    pub driver: Driver,
    /// Do not treat the target as a directory.
    pub no_target_directory: bool,
    /// Copy into a subdirectory of the target.
    pub target_directory: Option<PathBuf>,
    /// Sync each file after writing.
    pub fsync: bool,
    /// Reflink handling.
    pub reflink: ReflinkMode,
    /// Backup policy.
    pub backup: BackupMode,
}

fn build_command() -> clap::Command {
    clap::Command::new("xcp")
        .version(VERSION)
        .about("A (partial) clone of the Unix `cp` command with progress and pluggable drivers.")
        .arg(
            clap::Arg::new("paths")
                .num_args(0..)
                .help("Path list")
                .long_help(
                    "Path list.\n\nSource and destination files, or multiple source(s) to a directory.",
                ),
        )
        .arg(
            clap::Arg::new("verbose")
                .short('v')
                .long("verbose")
                .action(clap::ArgAction::Count)
                .help("Verbosity")
                .long_help("Verbosity.\n\nCan be specified multiple times to increase logging."),
        )
        .arg(
            clap::Arg::new("recursive")
                .short('r')
                .long("recursive")
                .action(clap::ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Copy directories recursively"),
        )
        .arg(
            clap::Arg::new("dereference")
                .short('L')
                .long("dereference")
                .action(clap::ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Dereference symlinks in source")
                .long_help(
                    "Dereference symlinks in source\n\nFollow symlinks, possibly recursively, when copying source files.",
                ),
        )
        .arg(
            clap::Arg::new("workers")
                .short('w')
                .long("workers")
                .num_args(1)
                .value_parser(clap::value_parser!(usize))
                .default_value("4")
                .help("Number of parallel workers")
                .long_help(
                    "Number of parallel workers.\n\nDefault is 4; if the value is negative or 0 it uses the number of logical CPUs.",
                ),
        )
        .arg(
            clap::Arg::new("block-size")
                .long("block-size")
                .num_args(1)
                .value_parser(parse_block_size)
                .default_value("1MB")
                .help("Block size for operations")
                .long_help(
                    "Block size for operations.\n\nAccepts standard size modifiers like \"M\" and \"GB\". Actual usage internally depends on the driver.",
                ),
        )
        .arg(
            clap::Arg::new("no-clobber")
                .short('n')
                .long("no-clobber")
                .action(clap::ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Do not overwrite an existing file"),

import os, pty, sys, select, time, subprocess, termios, struct, fcntl, re
cols=int(sys.argv[1]); wait=float(sys.argv[2]); out=sys.argv[3]; cmd=sys.argv[4:]

p=subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdin=s, stdout=s, stderr=s, close_fds=True)
t0=time.time(); buf=bytearray()
while time.time()-t0<wait and p.poll() is None:
    r,_,_=select.select([m],[],[],0.02)

p.kill()
data=bytes(buf)

actions.command:
cd /tmp/t4 && python3 - <<'EOF'
import os, pty, select, time, subprocess, termios, struct, fcntl
def run(b, bs):
    m,s=pty.openpty()
    fcntl.ioctl(s, termios.TIOCSWINSZ, struct.pack('HHHH', 24, 100, 0,0))
    os.set_blocking(m, False)
    if os.path.exists('/tmp/t4/oT3'): os.remove('/tmp/t4/oT3')
    t=time.perf_counter()
    p=subprocess.Popen([b,'--reflink','never','--block-size',bs,'med','/tmp/t4/oT3'], stdin=s, stdout=s, stderr=s, close_fds=True)
    n=0
    while time.perf_counter()-t < 20 and p.poll() is None:
        r,_,_=select.select([m],[],[],0.02)
        if r:
            try: d=os.read(m,1<<20)
            except OSError: break
            n+=len(d)
    dt=time.perf_counter()-t
    p.kill()
    return dt, n
for b in ['/workspace/executable','/tmp/mybin']:
    for bs in ['1000','1']:
        dt,n=run(b,bs)
        print(b.split('/')[-1], bs, 'time %.4f'%dt, 'bytes', n)

        print(c,'single-line?', repr(d[:120])); continue
    i+=3
    j=d.find(b'\x1b[',i)

    print('cols=%3d bar=%d stats_len=%3d n=%2d n*cols=%3d'%(c,c,len(stats),n,n*c))
PY"}

fn copy_data(
    from: &File,
    to: &File,
    info: &fsops::SourceInfo,
    opts: &CopyOpts,
    reporter: &Reporter,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    log::debug!("Attempting reflink from {:?}->{:?}", from, to);
    if reflink(from, to) {
        return Ok(());
    }
    match opts.reflink {
        ReflinkMode::Always => {
            return Err(Error::new(
                COPY,
                format!(
                    "Failed to reflink file and 'always' was specified: {:?}->{:?}",
                    from, to
                ),
            ));
        }
        _ => {}
    }
    log::debug!("Failed to reflink, falling back to copy");
    let size = info.size;
    let chunk = opts.block_size.max(1024 * 1024);
    let mut pos: u64 = 0;
    let mut reported: u64 = 0;
    while pos < size {
        let want = std::cmp::min(chunk, size - pos);
        let n = copy_range(from, pos, to, pos, want)?;
        if n == 0 {
            break;
        }
        pos += n;
        while reported < pos {
            let step = std::cmp::min(opts.block_size, pos - reported);
            if step == 0 {
                break;
            }
            reporter.add(step)?;
            reported += step;
        }
    }
    while reported < size {
        let step = std::cmp::min(opts.block_size, size - reported);
        if step == 0 {
            break;
        }
        reporter.add(step)?;
</output>

/// Expand filename patterns into the list of files they match.
fn expand_globs(patterns: &[PathBuf]) -> Result<Vec<PathBuf>, Error> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    for p in patterns {
        let pat = p.to_string_lossy();
        match glob::glob(&pat) {
            Ok(paths) => {
                for entry in paths {
                    if let Ok(path) = entry {
                        out.push(path);
                    }
                }
            }
            Err(e) => return Err(Error::new("", e.to_string())),
        }
    }
    Ok(out)
}

/// Compare two paths the way Rust's `Path` equality does (component wise).
fn same_path(a: &Path, b: &Path) -> bool {
    a == b
}
